notes.meaning: Azmaveth was a small town in the territory of Benjamin, just north of Jerusalem. Forty-two people from this town chose to make the long journey back from Babylon. Even though their hometown was small, every person who returned was carefully recorded.

These three towns had ancient roots near Jerusalem and were once associated with the Gibeonites. Because the groups returning to each separate village were small, they were counted together as one total of 743 people. They were willing to leave comfort behind to resettle their ruined ancestral homes.

Ramah and Geba were well-known towns in the land of Benjamin with rich histories in Israel. Together, 621 people returned to rebuild these communities. Their return helped restore life to the northern area just outside Jerusalem.

Michmash was famous as the site of a daring battle fought by King Saul and his son Jonathan. A group of 122 men returned to this rocky town. They were eager to live on the very ground where God had once delivered their ancestors.

Bethel and Ai were towns known since the days of Abraham and Joshua. A total of 223 men returned to resettle these historic places. God brought His people back to the very hills where He had made promises to their forefathers centuries before.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that Nehemiah 7:32 lists 123 people instead of 223, which is best explained as a copyist error during the copying of ancient manuscripts.

notes.meaning: This Nebo was a town in Judah, not the famous mountain in Moab. Only 52 people returned from this location. Even small groups received an honored place in God's public record.
Magbish refers to a family clan rather than a known town. A total of 156 relatives from this family joined the return. God remembered their name and their devotion in choosing to come home.

A second family group named Elam returned, numbering 1,254 people. The writer calls them the other Elam to avoid confusion with the family mentioned earlier in the list. Both clans had the same number of returnees and shared the same zeal to rebuild their homeland.

A clan named Harim brought 320 people back from exile. This group was an ordinary family, not to be confused with the priestly family of the same name. Each separate household had its own distinct part in reviving the nation.

Lod, Hadid, and Ono were located along the coastal plain, farther from Jerusalem than most other returning groups. A total of 725 people moved back to these towns. This shows that the exiles did not just crowd near Jerusalem, but also revived farming towns across the broader region.

Jericho was the famous city near the Jordan River that Joshua had conquered long ago. Three hundred forty-five men returned to its valley. These families later helped rebuild the city and construct the walls of Jerusalem.

Senaah formed the largest single clan in the entire list of ordinary citizens, with 3,630 members. This large group provided much-needed strength and numbers for the returning community. Their size made them an important source of labor and support for rebuilding.

The list now shifts from ordinary citizens to the tribe of Levi, beginning with the priests who led worship and offered sacrifices. Jedaiah belonged to the family line connected with the high priest. With 973 members returning, this family stepped forward to re-establish sacred worship in Jerusalem.

Immer was the name of one of the original priestly divisions organized by King David. A large company of 1,052 priests from this family returned. They gave up settled lives in Babylon to restore temple duties in their homeland.

Pashhur was a major priestly family that grew large after the days of David. They sent 1,247 priests back to Judah, making them the largest priestly group in the entire return. Their large number ensured there would be enough leaders to manage the altar and sanctuary.

This Harim was a priestly clan, distinct from the lay family named Harim mentioned earlier. A total of 1,017 priests returned under this name. Altogether, only four of David's original twenty-four priestly orders came back from Babylon, but their numbers were still very strong.

The Levites were the tribe chosen to assist the priests and care for the house of God. Surprisingly, only 74 Levites returned, representing just two families. Many Levites had grown comfortable in Babylon and did not want to take on the hard labor of starting over.

Singers were Levites appointed to lead the congregation in praise with voices and musical instruments. All 128 singers who returned belonged to the family of Asaph, the famous songwriter from King David's day. Their presence ensured that the psalms would once again be sung at the temple site.

The gatekeepers guarded the doors and storehouses of the temple to keep sacred spaces safe and orderly. Six families sent a combined total of 139 gatekeepers back to Jerusalem. Several of these families had carried out this exact same duty in the first temple before it was destroyed.

The temple servants, also known as the Nethinim, were workers dedicated to helping the Levites with daily physical tasks. They did practical work like chopping firewood, carrying water for sacrifices, and keeping the temple grounds clean. Nine family branches are named here, showing how God values even the humblest forms of service in His house.

The list of temple servants continues with six more family lines who traveled back with the community. Though their ancestors were likely foreigners given to serve at the altar, they had embraced the worship of Israel's God. Their devotion led them to leave Babylon so they could serve at the rebuilt house of the Lord.
